data.title: Tuberous sclerosis complex — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Tuberous sclerosis complex** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. Define tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC).**
- Autosomal dominant multisystem disorder (1 in 6000) with hamartomas in skin, brain, kidneys, heart, lungs and eyes, due to mutations in TSC1 (hamartin, 9q34) or TSC2 (tuberin, 16p13 — more severe) → loss of inhibition of mTORC1 (mammalian target of rapamycin) → cell growth; ~2/3 de novo
- Classic Vogt triad: seizures, intellectual disability, facial angiofibromas (epiloia) — present in <50%

**Q2. Describe the clinical features, criteria and diagnosis (PYQ) — 2021 criteria.**
- Major (11): hypomelanotic macules (≥3, ≥5 mm), angiofibromas (≥3) or fibrous cephalic plaque, ungual fibromas (≥2), shagreen patch, multiple retinal hamartomas, multiple cortical tubers and/or radial migration lines, subependymal nodules (≥2), subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA), cardiac rhabdomyoma, lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), angiomyolipomas (≥2)
- Minor (5): 'confetti' skin lesions, dental enamel pits (>3), intraoral fibromas (≥2), retinal achromic patch, multiple renal cysts, non-renal hamartomas, sclerotic bone lesions
- Definite TSC: 2 major or 1 major + ≥2 minor features, or identification of a pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variant; possible: 1 major or ≥2 minor (LAM + angiomyolipomas alone = need another feature)

**Q3. Write a short note on adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas) (PYQ).**
- Misnomer — they are angiofibromas (not sebaceous adenomas): symmetrical, smooth, red-pink, dome-shaped papules on nasolabial folds, cheeks and chin (sparing upper lip), appearing at 2–5 years and increasing at puberty; ~75–90% of TSC
- Histology: dermal fibrosis with stellate fibroblasts, dilated capillaries, absent elastic tissue, atrophic follicles
- Treatment: topical sirolimus (rapamycin 0.1–1%) — first line; PDL, CO2/Er:YAG laser ablation, shave excision, electrosurgery

**Q4. Write a short note on the shagreen patch (PYQ).**
- Connective tissue naevus (collagenoma): irregular, slightly elevated, skin-coloured to yellowish-brown plaque with orange-peel ('pig-skin'/shagreen leather) surface, usually on the lumbosacral area; appears in early childhood (~50% of TSC)
- Histology: thickened, densely packed collagen bundles in dermis

**Q5. Other skin signs.**
- Hypomelanotic macules (earliest sign — at birth; ash-leaf shape, polygonal 'thumbprint', confetti macules on limbs; best seen with Wood's lamp; poliosis)
- Fibrous cephalic plaque (forehead — yellowish-brown plaque, often first facial sign)
- Ungual fibromas (Koenen's tumours — periungual/subungual flesh-coloured papules after puberty, toenails > fingernails; longitudinal groove in nail)
- Intraoral (gingival) fibromas, dental enamel pits, molluscum pendulum, café-au-lait macules (not specific)

**Q6. Systemic manifestations.**
- CNS: cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, SEGA (obstructive hydrocephalus), seizures (infantile spasms — West syndrome), intellectual disability, autism, TAND (TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders)
- Kidney: angiomyolipomas (bleeding — leading cause of death in adults), cysts (TSC2/PKD1 contiguous gene syndrome), renal cell carcinoma
- Heart: rhabdomyomas (fetal/neonatal — regress), arrhythmias (WPW)
- Lungs: lymphangioleiomyomatosis (women — pneumothorax, chylothorax), multifocal micronodular pneumocyte hyperplasia
- Eyes: retinal hamartomas ('mulberry'), achromic patches

**Q7. Investigations and surveillance.**
- MRI brain (every 1–3 years until 25 y — SEGA), EEG, renal MRI (every 1–3 years), echocardiography and ECG (infancy), HRCT chest (women ≥18 y), ophthalmology, dental exam, neuropsychiatric assessment; genetic testing; examine parents

**Q8. Management.**
- mTOR inhibitors: everolimus (SEGA, angiomyolipomas, refractory seizures), sirolimus (LAM; topical for angiofibromas)
- Vigabatrin for infantile spasms; other antiepileptics; epilepsy surgery
- Embolisation/nephron-sparing surgery for bleeding angiomyolipomas
- Skin: topical sirolimus, lasers, excision of ungual fibromas and shagreen patches if symptomatic
- Genetic counselling (50% risk; germline mosaicism in apparently unaffected parents)

**Q9. Classify multiple tumour syndromes (PYQ).**
- With adnexal tumours: Cowden (trichilemmomas, acral keratoses, oral papillomas — PTEN; breast/thyroid/endometrial cancer), Muir–Torre (sebaceous neoplasms + visceral cancers — mismatch repair), Brooke–Spiegler/familial cylindromatosis (CYLD — cylindromas, spiradenomas, trichoepitheliomas), Birt–Hogg–Dubé (fibrofolliculomas, renal tumours, pneumothorax — FLCN), Gorlin (BCCs), Rombo, Bazex–Dupré–Christol
- With fibrous/neural/vascular tumours: TSC, NF1/NF2, Gardner (epidermoid cysts, osteomas, desmoids, colonic polyps — APC), MEN 2B (mucosal neuromas), Carney complex, Reed syndrome (multiple cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas + renal cell carcinoma — fumarate hydratase), blue rubber bleb, Maffucci

**Q10. Explain the genetics and molecular basis.**
- Autosomal dominant; TSC1 (hamartin, 9q34) or TSC2 (tuberin, 16p13 — more severe, ~70%); two-thirds are de novo
- Hamartin–tuberin complex inhibits Rheb → mTORC1; loss → mTOR overactivation → cell growth, hamartomas in skin, brain, kidney, heart, lung — basis of mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus)
- TSC2–PKD1 contiguous gene deletion → early severe polycystic kidney disease

**Q11. Give the 2021 updated diagnostic criteria (International TSC Consensus).**
- Major (11): hypomelanotic macules (≥3, ≥5 mm), angiofibromas (≥3) or fibrous cephalic plaque, ungual fibromas (≥2), shagreen patch, multiple retinal hamartomas, multiple cortical tubers and/or radial migration lines, subependymal nodules (≥2), subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, cardiac rhabdomyoma, lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), angiomyolipomas (≥2)
- Minor (7): 'confetti' skin lesions, dental enamel pits (>3), intraoral fibromas (≥2), retinal achromic patch, multiple renal cysts, non-renal hamartomas, sclerotic bone lesions
- Definite: 2 major or 1 major + ≥2 minor, or pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variant; possible: 1 major or ≥2 minor (LAM + AML alone doesn't count as definite)

**Q12. Describe the hypomelanotic macules in detail.**
- Earliest skin sign — at birth/infancy in ~90%: ash-leaf (lance-ovate), polygonal, thumbprint, confetti (tiny 1–3 mm on extremities); better seen with Wood's lamp; also poliosis (white hair tuft)
- Histology: normal melanocyte number with reduced melanin and smaller melanosomes

**Q13. Facial angiofibromas — treatment.**
- Appear at 3–10 years, increase at puberty: red papules on nasolabial folds, cheeks, chin (sparing upper lip)
- Topical sirolimus (rapamycin) 0.1–1% gel/ointment daily — first-line, best when started early; maintenance needed
- Procedures: pulsed-dye laser (erythema), CO2/ Er:YAG ablation, shave/ electrosurgery, dermabrasion for established fibrotic lesions; recurrence common

**Q14. What are ungual fibromas (Koenen tumours)?**
- Flesh-coloured firm papules emerging from proximal nail fold (periungual) or under the nail (subungual) — appear after puberty; produce longitudinal nail groove; more on toes; treated by excision when painful; single lesion can occur after trauma in normal people

**Q15. Describe the neurological features.**
- Epilepsy in ~85% (infantile spasms in ~1/3 — vigabatrin first-line; drug-resistant epilepsy common; everolimus, cannabidiol, epilepsy surgery), cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, SEGA (near foramen of Monro — hydrocephalus; everolimus/ surgery), TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders (TAND — intellectual disability, autism, ADHD, anxiety)

**Q16. Renal and pulmonary features.**
- Angiomyolipomas (~80% adults) — risk of haemorrhage when >3 cm (Wunderlich syndrome); treat with everolimus or embolisation; renal cysts, renal cell carcinoma (rare), CKD
- Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) — women of reproductive age, cystic lung disease, pneumothorax, chylous effusion; sirolimus stabilises lung function

**Q17. Cardiac rhabdomyomas — relevance.**
- Detected antenatally (often the first clue to TSC on fetal echo); usually regress in infancy; may cause arrhythmias (WPW) or outflow obstruction in neonates

**Q18. Ophthalmic and dental features.**
- Retinal astrocytic hamartomas ('mulberry' or flat translucent), retinal achromic patches; dental enamel pits (best seen with dental dye), gingival fibromas — oral exam essential

**Q19. What is the fibrous cephalic plaque?**
- Raised, yellow-brown/ skin-coloured rubbery plaque on forehead/scalp (collagenoma) — often the first visible lesion after hypomelanotic macules; counts as major criterion with angiofibromas

**Q20. Surveillance recommendations.**
- Brain MRI every 1–3 years until age 25 (SEGA), EEG in infants (subclinical seizures), TAND screening yearly, abdominal MRI every 1–3 years for AML, BP and renal function yearly, chest HRCT in women at 18 y (LAM), ECG/echo at baseline, dermatology and dental review yearly, ophthalmology baseline

**Q21. Differential diagnosis of facial angiofibromas.**
- Acne vulgaris (comedones, pustules), rosacea, trichoepitheliomas (Brooke–Spiegler), Birt–Hogg–Dubé fibrofolliculomas, MEN1 angiofibromas, multiple syringomas, sebaceous adenomas (Muir–Torre), tricholemmomas (Cowden)

**Q22. What is the histopathology of angiofibroma and shagreen patch?**
- Angiofibroma: dermal fibrosis with stellate/ plump fibroblasts, dilated vessels, perifollicular fibrosis, atrophic follicles
- Shagreen patch: connective tissue naevus (collagenoma) — thickened dense collagen bundles, reduced elastic fibres

**Q23. Systemic mTOR inhibitors — use and side effects.**
- Everolimus: SEGA, renal AML (>3 cm), refractory epilepsy; sirolimus: LAM; also improve skin lesions
- Side effects: stomatitis/ mouth ulcers, acne-like eruptions, hyperlipidaemia, hyperglycaemia, infections, impaired wound healing, proteinuria, pneumonitis

**Q24. Genetic counselling in TSC.**
- 50% risk to offspring of affected parent; de novo in ~2/3 but parents should be examined (mild features, gonadal mosaicism ~2%); prenatal/ pre-implantation testing possible

**Q25. How does TSC present at different ages?**
- Fetus/newborn: cardiac rhabdomyoma, hypomelanotic macules
- Infancy: infantile spasms, developmental delay, ash-leaf macules
- Childhood: angiofibromas, shagreen patch, autism/ learning difficulties
- Adolescence/adult: ungual fibromas, renal AML, LAM in women

**Q26. Classify multiple tumour/ hamartoma syndromes with skin markers.**
- TSC (angiofibromas), NF1 (neurofibromas), Cowden/ PTEN hamartoma (trichilemmomas, acral keratoses, oral papillomas — breast/thyroid/endometrial cancer), Birt–Hogg–Dubé (fibrofolliculomas — renal cancer, pneumothorax), Gorlin (BCCs, palmar pits), Muir–Torre (sebaceous tumours — colorectal cancer), Gardner (epidermoid cysts, osteomas — colon polyps), MEN1 (angiofibromas, collagenomas), MEN2B (mucosal neuromas), Carney complex (lentigines, myxomas), Brooke–Spiegler (cylindromas, trichoepitheliomas)

**Q27. What is the prognosis?**
- Variable; main causes of morbidity/mortality — renal disease (AML haemorrhage, CKD), status epilepticus/ SUDEP, SEGA, LAM; most live into adulthood with surveillance

## Quick spotter facts
- Facial angiofibromas + ash-leaf macules + shagreen patch + Koenen's tumours — tuberous sclerosis (mTOR)
- Topical sirolimus for angiofibromas; everolimus for SEGA/AML

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Tuberous sclerosis); 2021 International TSC Consensus diagnostic criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
